title: The promise by the river
hookLine: Karna has Yudhishthira beaten, and lets him go
carry: vachan: a word kept, even unseen

cards: Yudhishthira's bow is cut. His chariot is wrecked. He is the eldest of the Pandavas, the man the whole war is being fought to crown, and he stands beaten, within reach of Karna's weapons.
One more arrow would do it. And Karna lowers his weapon. He mocks Yudhishthira, tells him to go back to his own kind and leave fighting to warriors, and he lets him go.
In the epic he spares Nakula, one of the twins, the same way. Why?

teach.b: The answer is back before the war, by a riverbank. Karna used to pray facing the sun, and one day, as he finished, a woman was standing in his shadow. It was Kunti, the mother of the Pandavas.
She told him what he had never known for certain: she was his mother too. She had borne him as a girl, before her marriage, a son of the sun god, and set him afloat on the river.
Now she asked him to come over to his brothers' side. Karna refused. Where were you, he says in effect, when I needed a mother?
Duryodhana stood by me when no one else did, and I won't leave him now. But he gave Kunti something. He promised he would not kill her sons, except Arjuna.
One of the two of us will die, he told her, and either way you'll keep your sons. So on the field, with Yudhishthira at his mercy, Karna remembers the riverbank. Here's the part that aches.
Karna knows, and Kunti knows, and so does Krishna, who had told him of his birth. To Yudhishthira, Karna is just the enemy who mocked him and let him live.
The brothers don't know they are being spared by their own brother.
Hindu families have a word for what Karna keeps: vachan, a given word. Tulsidas's Ramayana, sung in many homes, puts it in one line: life may go, but the word must not.
Karna keeps his with no one watching and no one to thank him.

how: The meeting of Kunti and Karna by the river is retold in readings, plays and poems, and Karna's choice to stay with Duryodhana is discussed in Hindu homes and classrooms as a hard question about loyalty and duty.

o: Kunti's firstborn, who keeps a secret promise to his mother
a son of the sun who goes over to his brothers' side
the eldest Pandava, spared on the field by his enemy

s: Karna agreed to join his brothers once Kunti told him the truth
he refused; he would not leave Duryodhana.
Karna promised Kunti not to kill her sons, except Arjuna
and on the field he keeps that promise.
Yudhishthira knew why Karna spared him
the brothers didn't know Karna was their brother.

games.q: you're Karna. Yudhishthira stands beaten in front of you, and one arrow would end the war. what do you do?
o: mock him, and let him go.
games.why: Karna mocks him and lets him go, keeping his vachan to Kunti by the river, though no one on the field knows why.

practice: Karna made his promise just after his prayer to the sun, the way many Hindus still offer water to the sun in the morning. Let your shoulders drop and breathe out slowly.

Bring to mind a promise you carry that nobody else can see, and hold it the way you'd hold something fragile in both hands. If you pray, you can renew it in your prayer; if not, just hold it a moment longer.

wordCard.voice: Karna. The warrior who could have ended the war with one arrow, and kept a promise to his mother instead, while his brothers never knew why.

orig.note: Kunti: mother of the Pandavas, and, in secret, of Karna.

carryVoice: Your line: vachan: a word kept, even unseen. A promise to a mother, kept in secret. That's day eight hundred thirty-nine.
